A subplot is a secondary story that runs alongside the main story inside a larger narrative — a novel, film, TV show, play, or any other form of storytelling.

Every story has a main plot: the central conflict, the primary question the story is built around, the core journey. This is the spine of the story — everything else holds onto it.

A subplot is a smaller, supporting story that happens at the same time, within the same story world. It is not the main focus, but it is a real, developed story of its own — not just a passing detail.

Think of it this way: the main plot is the highway a story travels on. A subplot is a side road that branches off from it — it has its own scenery and its own little journey, but it always stays connected to the larger trip.
A subplot has its own story shape

This is what separates a subplot from just something that happens. A subplot has:

  • A beginning — it gets introduced
  • A middle — it develops, faces complications
  • An end — it reaches a resolution or turning point

If a character mentions their sick father once and it's never brought up again, that's just a detail. For something to be a subplot, the story must follow it across multiple scenes, tracking it toward some kind of outcome.

Imagine a detective thriller. The main plot is: Detective Meera is racing to catch a serial killer before they strike again.

Running alongside that:

  • Meera's marriage is quietly falling apart because she's consumed by the case. → Subplot 1
  • Meera's partner is secretly hiding a piece of evidence because someone is blackmailing him. → Subplot 2
  • Two junior officers on the team fall in love while working long nights together. → Subplot 3

None of these is the murder mystery. But all of them are unfolding at the same time, in the same story. And in a well-written story, they connect — the blackmailed partner's secret collides with the main plot at a critical moment; Meera's marriage fractures right as she's most vulnerable; the romance provides warmth in an otherwise dark story.

1. To develop secondary characters.
The main plot can only give so much attention to anyone other than the central character. Subplots give side characters space to grow, struggle, and change. Without them, most characters stay flat.

2. To make the story world feel real.
In real life, multiple things happen at the same time. Subplots recreate that — the world doesn't pause while the main conflict plays out. This gives stories texture and life.

3. To explore themes more deeply.
Often a subplot mirrors or contrasts the main plot's themes. If the main plot is about a character learning to forgive, a subplot might follow another character who refuses to forgive — and shows the cost of that. The two stories together say something bigger than either one could alone.

4. To create emotional variety.
A tense, dark main plot might have a lighter subplot to give the audience breathing room. That contrast makes both feel more powerful. This is why a tragedy often has comic moments — they're usually tucked into subplots.

5. To influence the main plot.
The best subplots don't just run separately — they affect the main story. Something a character learns or experiences in a subplot gives them the ability, knowledge, or courage to resolve the main conflict. The subplot earns its place by feeding back into the highway.
How many subplots can a story have?

As many as the author chooses, though a typical novel or film usually has 1–3. A long-running TV series might have dozens across its run.

In TV writing, writers often call these "the A story, B story, and C story." The A story is the main plot. The B story and C story are the subplots. This language is so common in screenwriting that "B plot" and "subplot" are used interchangeably.
Subplot across different types of stories

The word applies equally to:

  • Novels — a character's private romance running alongside the main adventure
  • Films — a secondary character's journey toward redemption
  • TV shows — each episode's B plot and C plot
  • Plays — Shakespeare's plays are especially famous for richly interwoven subplots (in Hamlet, the main plot is Hamlet's revenge; subplots include Ophelia's mental collapse and Laertes' own quest for vengeance)
  • Video games with stories — side quests that have their own narrative arc
The word used outside of fiction

People also use "subplot" metaphorically in real life, to describe secondary developments happening beneath the surface of a larger situation:

"The company merger is the main news, but there's a whole subplot about which senior leaders are quietly positioning themselves for the top role."

"The election dominated the headlines, but the real subplot was the growing divide within the party itself."

Here, "subplot" treats real events like a story — it means: a secondary set of developments, motivations, or tensions that is unfolding behind or beneath the main, visible story.

A subplot is a secondary storyline within a larger narrative. It has its own arc (beginning, development, resolution), it usually focuses on secondary characters, and it runs alongside the main plot. Good subplots are not independent extras — they connect to the main plot, deepen its themes, develop its characters, and make the story feel like a real and full world rather than a single narrow thread. The word also travels into everyday language, where it means any secondary set of events quietly unfolding beneath the main action.
